title: A confidence ellipse is a level set of the covariance, and dropping a parameter changes its size in a predictable direction
summary: Three figures show a joint uncertainty ellipsoid reduced to two parameters in two different ways: its shadow (marginal) and its slice (conditional). The conditional ellipse always sits inside the marginal one, and sampling from the wrong matrix factor draws a cloud of the wrong size.

media.alt: Two panels of nested ellipses on axes DeltaA over sigma_A and Delta n over sigma_n, both from minus one to one. Left, titled correlated: a large tilted red ellipse with a smaller blue dashed ellipse inside it, touching it on the upper left and lower right. Right, titled uncorrelated: the red and blue ellipses coincide.

source.caption: Ellipsoid containment (sampling validity)
source.note: Group explainer: the representative figure is the first; the other two are read the same way. Only standard Gaussian and linear-algebra theory is taught here; the project's own sampling procedure is not described.
group: 01_fig1_ellipsoid_containment: Ellipsoid containment (sampling validity): marginal versus conditional ellipse, correlated and uncorrelated cases
02_fig2_projection: Projection onto reduced parameter space: the 3D ellipsoid, its shadow on the floor and its cross-section, plus the 2D view
03_fig3_sampling_validity: Sampling validity check: a correct and an incorrect Cholesky factor, each with a sample cloud and 2-sigma ellipses

read_the_figure.question: If a three-parameter uncertainty region is reduced to two parameters, which two-dimensional region is the right one, and how can a sampler be checked against it?
read_the_figure.axes: Both axes are deviations from nominal, divided by their own standard deviation (DeltaA over sigma_A, Delta n over sigma_n; in the third figure Delta n and Delta E_a). A value of 1 therefore means one standard deviation. Red solid = marginal ellipse (the shadow). Blue dashed = conditional ellipse (the slice). In figure 3 the dots are samples and the ellipses are 2-sigma contours.
look_at: Is the blue dashed ellipse inside the red one everywhere? In the left panel it is, and it touches the red outline on the upper-left and lower-right.
In the right panel (labelled uncorrelated) the two outlines lie on top of each other: nothing is lost by slicing instead of projecting.
In figure 2 the left 3D view shows why: the purple ellipsoid casts a shadow on the floor (red) and is cut by a horizontal plane (blue dashed). The shadow is the bigger outline.

In figure 3, left: the dashed contour of the sampled matrix lies exactly on the solid target. Right: the dashed contour is smaller than the target, and the dots are drawn from it, so the cloud is too small.
read_the_figure.proves: That a conditional (slice) ellipse can never be larger than the marginal (shadow) ellipse of the same level, that the two are equal only when the removed parameter is uncorrelated with the kept ones, and that a sampler is valid only if its covariance reproduces the target ellipse.
if_wrong: A blue ellipse that pokes outside the red one: the two are not computed from the same covariance and level, or the axes are not normalised the same way.
Two ellipses that coincide in a case labelled correlated: the cross-covariance has been set to zero somewhere.
A dashed sampling contour that is smaller than the target (figure 3, right): the matrix factor was built from the wrong block, so the samples under-represent the uncertainty.
must_check: The same contour level (here 1 sigma in figures 1 and 2, 2 sigma in figure 3) is used for every ellipse being compared.
Axes are normalised or share one scale, otherwise a tilted ellipse cannot be read by eye.
Which parameter is removed is stated (figure titles: E_a in figures 1 and 2, A in figure 3).
The figure says whether it shows a projection or a slice: they are different objects with different sizes.
A contour legend names the matrix each outline was computed from.
as_drawn: Read by eye, the red ellipse in figure 1 (right) reaches about plus and minus 1 on both axes, which is what a 1-sigma ellipse of a covariance matrix does (its bounding box is plus and minus sigma).

In figure 3 (left) the 2-sigma contour reaches about plus and minus 2 on the Delta n axis (and about 2 on Delta E_a), as expected for a 2-sigma ellipse in normalised units; the dots extend beyond it, as they should (a 2-sigma ellipse does not hold all samples).

The panel title symbol Sigma_12 is not defined on the figure. It is read here as the coupling between the kept pair and the removed parameter; that is the quantity that decides whether the two ellipses differ.

terms.meaning: A symmetric table of variances (diagonal) and covariances (off-diagonal) of the parameters. It fully describes the spread of a Gaussian cloud.
The level set of the Gaussian quadratic form: all points whose squared Mahalanobis distance from the centre is at most c. Two parameters give an ellipse, three an ellipsoid.
The distribution of a subset of parameters when the others are ignored (integrated out). Its covariance is simply the matching sub-block of the full matrix.
The distribution of a subset of parameters when the others are held at known values. It is narrower than the marginal whenever they are correlated.
The block of Sigma that couples the kept parameters I to the removed ones R. When it is zero the two ellipses coincide.
A lower-triangular matrix L with L L^T = Sigma. A sampler draws z from a unit Gaussian and returns L z, which then has covariance Sigma.
A deviation from nominal divided by its own standard deviation, so that the unit on every axis is one sigma.
For matrices, M1 is at least M2 if M1 minus M2 never makes a quadratic form negative. It is the matrix version of 'bigger than' and decides which ellipse contains which.

remember: An ellipse x^T S^-1 x = c has a bounding box of plus and minus sqrt(c S_ii) on axis i: for c = 1 each axis extent is exactly the standard deviation.
Marginal means 'ignore the other parameters' and keeps the sub-block of Sigma. Conditional means 'fix the other parameters' and subtracts a non-negative correction.
Slice inside shadow: knowing a correlated parameter can only shrink the uncertainty of the others.
The inverse of a sub-block is not the sub-block of the inverse, so never mix covariance and precision blocks.
A Cholesky factor belongs to the matrix it was computed from: a sub-block of L is not the factor of the sub-block of Sigma.

understand.title: Why two different ellipses exist at all
understand.text: A joint three-parameter region has two natural two-parameter reductions. If you do not know the third parameter, you must allow for all of its values: that is the shadow, the marginal. If you have pinned the third parameter at its nominal value, you only see the cross-section through the middle: the conditional. The 3D picture in figure 2 makes the difference visible: the shadow is the outline of the whole solid, the slice is its cut.

understand.title: Why correlation is what separates them
understand.text: If the removed parameter is independent of the others, fixing it tells you nothing and the cut has the same shape as the shadow (figure 1, right). If it is correlated, fixing it tells you where the others probably are, so the cut is smaller (figure 1, left). The more correlated, the bigger the gap.

understand.title: The sampling check
understand.text: A sampler that claims to represent an ellipse can be tested by overlaying the ellipse of its own covariance on the target and on the sample cloud. Figure 3 does exactly that for a correct and an incorrect factor. The incorrect one is not random noise: it is systematically too narrow, because a piece of the covariance has been dropped.

steps.title: The ellipse as a level set
steps.note: For c = 1 the ellipse touches plus and minus sigma on each axis, which is why the red outline in figure 1 reaches about 1 on both normalised axes.

steps.title: Partition the parameters
steps.note: I is the kept set (two parameters here) and R the removed one. All later formulas only use these four blocks.

steps.title: The shadow uses the sub-block
steps.note: Projecting the ellipsoid onto the kept axes gives the ellipse of the matching sub-block of the covariance (the red outline). This is the standard marginal of a Gaussian.

steps.title: The slice uses the Schur complement
steps.note: Cutting at the removed parameter's nominal value leaves a region whose matrix is the inverse of the matching block of the precision matrix, and by the Schur-complement identity that is exactly this conditional covariance (the blue outline).

steps.title: Containment follows from a sign
steps.note: The subtracted term is non-negative, so the conditional covariance is smaller; taking inverses reverses the order, so every point of the conditional set also satisfies the marginal inequality. Equality holds when the cross-covariance is zero: the right panel of figure 1.

steps.title: One-dimensional size of the effect
steps.note: For one kept and one removed parameter with correlation rho, fixing the removed one shrinks the standard deviation by the factor sqrt(1 - rho^2). It is the quantity behind the gap between red and blue in the left panel.

steps.title: Sampling with a Cholesky factor
steps.note: This is the standard way to turn independent unit Gaussians into a correlated cloud. The factor must be the one of the matrix you want to reproduce.

steps.title: Why a sub-block of L is wrong
steps.note: If the removed parameter is ordered first, the kept rows of L also contain a column coupling them to it. Dropping that column removes the positive term l l^T, so the sampled covariance is smaller than the target. That is the dashed contour in figure 3, right.

worked.title: How much narrower is the slice for a correlation of 0.6?
worked.problem: Two standardised parameters (variance 1 each) have correlation 0.6. How wide is the conditional spread of one of them when the other is fixed, relative to its marginal spread?

solution.text: Conditional variance with variance 1 and correlation 0.6.
Take the square root to get the ratio of standard deviations.

worked.answer: The slice is 20 percent narrower along that axis than the shadow. The gap in the left panel grows with the correlation and vanishes at zero.

analyze.q: In figure 1, left, the blue ellipse touches the red one in two places. What does that say about the direction of the strongest dependence on the removed parameter?
analyze.hint: The gap is smallest along the direction in which the removed parameter has the least influence.

analyze.q: If the kept parameters were also uncorrelated with each other, how would the left panel look if the removed parameter were still correlated with them?
analyze.hint: The shadow would be an axis-aligned ellipse; the slice would still be smaller.

analyze.q: Figure 3 (right) uses a smaller matrix for sampling. Predict, without looking, what fraction of dots you would expect outside the 2-sigma target ellipse compared with the left panel.
analyze.hint: A smaller cloud puts fewer points outside a fixed contour.

evaluate.q: A reviewer says: 'the sampled cloud is inside the physically valid region, so the sampler is valid'. Using figure 3, explain why that test alone is not sufficient.
evaluate.hint: Both the correct and the too-small cloud are inside the target; validity is about reproducing the covariance, not about being contained.

evaluate.q: Which reduction (shadow or slice) is the honest one when the removed parameter is not known precisely? When is the slice acceptable?
evaluate.hint: Think about what you assume about the removed parameter in each case.

create: Sketch the version of figure 1 for a removed parameter with correlation 0.9 with both kept ones: where do the two ellipses touch, and how large is the gap?
Design a one-line numerical test that would have caught the wrong factor in figure 3 before any plot was drawn.

checks.q: Why is the conditional ellipse never larger than the marginal one?
checks.hint: Look at the sign of the correction term.
checks.answer: Because the conditional covariance equals the marginal covariance minus a positive semi-definite correction (the cross-covariance term). A smaller covariance has a smaller ellipse of the same level.

checks.q: Two parameters have correlation 0.8 and unit variance. By what factor does the standard deviation of one shrink when the other is fixed?
checks.answer: sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.6, so the spread shrinks to 60 percent of the marginal.

checks.q: In figure 1 (right) the ellipses coincide. What does that tell you about the cross-covariance and about the value of fixing the removed parameter?
checks.hint: Equality in the containment needs a zero correction.
checks.answer: The cross-covariance between kept and removed parameters is zero, so the correction term vanishes. Fixing the removed parameter tells you nothing about the kept ones: shadow and slice are the same ellipse.

checks.q: A sampler's samples fall visibly inside the target 2-sigma ellipse more often than 95 percent of the time. Is it valid?
checks.hint: For a 2D Gaussian the 2-sigma ellipse contains about 86 percent, not 95.
checks.answer: No, not by that evidence. For a 2D Gaussian the 2-sigma (Mahalanobis radius 2) ellipse contains 1 - exp(-2) = 86 percent of samples. A sampler that puts clearly more points inside it has a covariance that is too small, as in figure 3, right.

checks.q: How would you test numerically that a factor L reproduces a given covariance Sigma?
checks.hint: Compare L L^T to Sigma, and compare a sample covariance for large n.
checks.answer: Check that L @ L.T equals Sigma to round-off. Then draw many samples x = L z, compute their sample covariance, and confirm that it approaches Sigma with an error that falls as one over the square root of the number of samples.
